node.label: Ian McKay
node.date_label: Tartanism Triumphant 1992 · The Quest of the Folk 1994 · 'A Note on Region' and the liberal order prospectus 2000 · later readings 2005, 2008, 2009
node.description: Reads twentieth-century Nova Scotia's 'folk' as a cultural selection by folklorists, handicraft planners, writers and the tourist state, and as a local version of an international antimodernist wave (1992, 1994). In 2000 he proposed treating Canada as a project of liberal rule, to be studied through the implantation of liberalism across a heterogeneous terrain, and asked how 'region' fits that project. Later work turns to the Canadian left as a counter-project (2005, 2008) and answers the framework's critics (2009).
node.representative_figures_and_works: Ian McKay (b. 1953); “Tartanism Triumphant: The Construction of Scottishness in Nova Scotia, 1933–1954” (1992); The Quest of the Folk: Antimodernism and Cultural Selection in Twentieth-Century Nova Scotia (1994); “A Note on ‘Region’ in Writing the History of Atlantic Canada” (2000); “The Liberal Order Framework: A Prospectus for a Reconnaissance of Canadian History” (2000). Later readings: Rebels, Reds, Radicals (2005); Reasoning Otherwise (2008); “Canada as a Long Liberal Revolution” (2009). Further selected bibliography: With Jamie Swift, Warrior Nation: Rebranding Canada in an Age of Anxiety (2012); With Robin Bates, In the Province of History: The Making of the Public Past in Twentieth-Century Nova Scotia (2010).
node.scope_note: This entry presents the 1992 article and the 1994 book on antimodernism and the folk, and the two essays of 2000 on region and liberal order. The 1992 article is read at pp. 5–9 and 13–14; the 1994 book is checked at summary and contents level, with its closing argument (p. 306) quoted by Muise (1998); the region essay is read in full; the prospectus is checked at abstract level, with pp. 620–21 quoted by Fecteau (2009). The framework takes its name from his prospectus, but state-formation studies (Curtis 1988; Greer and Radforth 1992) precede it and commentators name Gramsci and Fernande Roy (1988) as its sources; he is not presented as the founder of a field. The 2005, 2008 and 2009 works are later readings. Canonical-work review (2026-10-24): added titles and dates are selected bibliography, not a complete career or a new reading of the books. Original works, translations, edited collections and posthumous editions are distinguished; earlier argument and source-reading qualifications remain.

incident_edges.relationship: Canada as a project of liberal rule: the prospectus of 2000
incident_edges.evidence_note: In-period evidence (2000). The prospectus abstract (read) proposes mapping 'the Canadian state as a project of liberal rule in northern North America' to get beyond the 'socio-cultural versus national-political impasse'. Its core formulation (pp. 620–21) is checked as quoted by Fecteau (2009): 'Canada-as-project can be analyzed through the study of the implantation and expansion over a heterogeneous terrain of a certain politico-economic logic – to wit liberalism.' The prospectus body is not read here. McKay's spring 2000 Acadiensis essay (pp. 90–91, read) sets out the same programme in his own words: 'a strategy of reconnaissance'; the project 'was the project of liberal order, a coherent attempt to install a liberal public philosophy and practice of "peace, order and good government" in northern North America'; 'Canada was thus a process, not a self-evident thing, and the key to this process was liberalization'. A contribution, not a founding: state-formation studies (Curtis 1988; Greer and Radforth 1992) precede it, and Pâquet (2009) names Gramsci and Fernande Roy (1988) as its sources. In the sampled corpus, 90 of 1,303 strict History doctoral dissertations dated 2009–2026 cite the prospectus. Bibliographies record consultation, not influence. The 2009 reply and the histories of the left (2005, 2008) are later readings, not evidence for this edge.

incident_edges.relationship: Antimodernism and the invented folk in twentieth-century Nova Scotia (1992, 1994)
incident_edges.evidence_note: In-period evidence (1992, 1994). In 'Tartanism Triumphant' (Acadiensis, 1992; pp. 5–9 read) McKay asks how Nova Scotia 'became Scottish' in the second quarter of the twentieth century, when 'a collection of hazy generalizations and ethnic stereotypes' became 'a natural and obvious "commonsense"'. His broad answer: 'it was part of an international anti-modernist wave, a local version of a general middle-class search for something outside and better than the crisis-ridden modern world it inhabited' (pp. 8–9); the narrow answer is the state's cultural power under Angus L. Macdonald. Note 12 takes Lears's definition of American antimodernism and adds the 'simple life' and 'nature'. The Quest of the Folk (1994) is checked at summary and contents level: chapters on 'The Idea of the Folk', Helen Creighton and folklore, Mary Black and handicrafts, the simple life, and the folk 'under conditions of postmodernity'. Muise's review essay (Acadiensis, 1998; pp. 128–32 read) describes the three case studies and quotes the book's conclusion that 'the concept of the Folk was and remains a powerful obstacle to the formation of a counter-hegemonic cultural politics' (p. 306). Wright's 1995 Acadiensis review essay on English-Canadian intellectual history cites the book for 'a very skilled handling of Antonio Gramsci's theory of cultural hegemony by an historian' (p. 132 n. 29). A contribution to the field's cultural strand, not its origin: Berger, McKillop and Owram precede it. In the sampled corpus, 56 of 1,303 strict History doctoral dissertations dated 2009–2026 cite the book. Bibliographies record consultation, not influence. In the Province of History (2010, with Bates) is a later reading.

incident_edges.relationship: Rethinking 'region' inside a history of the liberal project (2000)
incident_edges.evidence_note: In-period evidence (Acadiensis, spring 2000; pp. 89–101 read; a lightly edited version of a talk prepared for the August 1997 Atlantic Canada Workshop, dated here by publication). McKay finds that the 1990s 'multiplication of subject-positions, epistemologies and methodologies places a question mark over the very concept of an "Atlantic Canada"' (p. 90). He then asks where region fits a history of Canada as a liberal project and answers 'Quite centrally' (p. 95). He sets aside natural, essentialist definitions of the region (pp. 95–96); he finds heartland–hinterland and dependency models descriptively rich, but asks them to 'undergo the rigorous analysis of concepts' (pp. 96–99). He would resist a nationalizing historiography that reduces the region to one inferior term (p. 99). As an agenda he proposes exploring 'the remarkable extent to which Atlantic Canadians built the Canadian liberal project' (p. 99) and a regional 'communitarian critique of the liberal order' (p. 100). He also rejects the charge that regionalists are a 'balkanizing faction' (p. 91). This is a reconsideration from inside the field. In the sampled corpus, 4 of 1,303 strict History doctoral dissertations dated 2009–2026 cite the essay under its main record (one more under a variant record).

incident_edges.relationship: McKay's historical work is Gramscian by his own account: cultural hegemony in The Quest of the Folk (1994), and 'the Gramscian assumptions that have shaped my outlook' (2000)
incident_edges.evidence_note: McKay's own words, read in full ("A Note on 'Region' in Writing the History of Atlantic Canada", Acadiensis 29:2, 2000, p. 89): 'the Gramscian assumptions that have shaped my outlook'. Muise (Acadiensis 27:2, 1998, read pp. 124, 128–132) reports that in The Quest of the Folk McKay places himself 'within a neo-marxist framework associated with the work of Antonio Gramsci' and quotes the book (p. 306): 'the concept of the Folk was and remains a powerful obstacle to the formation of a counter-hegemonic cultural politics'. Wright (Acadiensis 24:2, 1995, p. 132 n. 29): 'For a very skilled handling of Antonio Gramsci's theory of cultural hegemony by an historian see Ian McKay, The Quest of the Folk'. Critic: Palmer (2009) argues that McKay's Gramsci conflates hegemony and domination. The Quest of the Folk is given through these readers. Distinct from edge_844 (Gramsci → the liberal order framework, 2000): this arrow carries the influence on McKay's work from 1994, before the prospectus.

named_group_routes.evidence_note: McKay (2000, pp. 89–90) contrasts the 1990s agenda of gender, ethnicity and community with "1970s and early-1980s topics" of regional underdevelopment and class conflict, and calls the new pluralism "a continuation of … the social-history revolution of the 1960s and 1970s". named_group_routes.relationship: National-political history as one side of the debate
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Contesting Clio's Craft (description) names "the political vs. social history debates that have dominated the field since the 1970s". PhD context: 24 of 34 2009–2026 PhDs citing a core debate text also engage the Political, international & national history anchor set (71% vs 19% of all; lift 3.8). named_group_routes.relationship: The liberal order framework is Gramscian: liberal order as hegemony and the national-political 'commonsense' (2000)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: McKay's abstract (2000) maps Canada as 'a project of liberal rule in northern North America' through which 'liberal order became the national-political ‘commonsense’'. Ajzenstat (2009) describes McKay as recommending 'a Gramscian approach to Canadian history'; Pâquet (2009) names Gramsci, with Fernande Roy (1988), as one of the prospectus's two explicit influences; Palmer (2009) argues that McKay's reading of Gramscian hegemony is too seamless, conflating hegemony and domination. McKay's own Gramscian outlook is drawn separately (gramsci → ian_mckay, revision 1.149). PhD context: 9 of the 91 PhDs citing McKay 2000 also cite a Gramsci work.

named_group_routes.relationship: Liberal order and capitalism: analytically separate, historically entangled
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Fecteau quotes McKay that liberalism and capitalism must be kept "analytically separate" (2000, 629) yet after the 1840s "could not be easily separated" (2009, 385), and quotes McKay in 1994 on a "liberal capitalist order … based on possessive individualism". A teaching comparison between historical-materialist categories and the framework, not a descent.

named_group_routes.relationship: Draws social and political history into a renewed political history
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Parnaby: McKay argued that liberalism as a "project of rule" could draw social and political history into one problematique, and interest in that question has reinvigorated histories of political ideas, institutions, census taking, border making and tax collecting. A contribution, not a claim that it founded political history in Canada.

named_group_routes.relationship: Liberal rule and moral regulation: neighbouring, distinct projects
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The user kept them apart (2026-10-12): the framework is "a different project closer to history of capitalism". Pâquet links the framework to studies of "liberal social regulation", and Valverde places moral reform at the centre of English Canada's race, class and gender organization. PhD context: 27 of 91 McKay-citing PhDs also cite Valverde (lift 3.6). Comparison only.

named_group_routes.relationship: Offers a way past the social versus national-political impasse
named_group_routes.evidence_note: McKay's abstract frames the prospectus as a way past "the present socio-cultural versus national-political impasse in Canadian history writing"; Ajzenstat sets it against Granatstein's attempt to revive national history. An intervention in the debate's terms, not a party to every exchange in it.

Curtis presents Ruling by Schooling Quebec as "A Historical Sociology" and Pâquet ties the framework to studies of state formation. Comparison only: no checked source links the Canadian work to the comparative historical sociology the atlas entry describes. Corrigan and Sayer's Great Arch is co-cited (6 of 10 citing PhDs also cite McKay 2000) but unread.

named_group_routes.relationship: Liberal order criticised as an elastic, seemingly trans-historical category that sidesteps capitalism's changing historical structures, in a review of McKay's Reasoning Otherwise (2009)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Dated 2009. 'Radical Reasoning', a feature review essay on Ian McKay, Reasoning Otherwise (2008), The Underhill Review (Carleton University), Fall 2009, read in full (web text; locators below are pages of the print PDF, https://www3.carleton.ca/underhillreview/09/fall/reviews/print/Palmer.pdf). He reads McKay's liberal order as a project 'in which liberty, equality, and private property are sanctified as the foundations of a civil society that valorizes individualism', and says past leftists 'never spoke of an enemy that they named "liberal order."' 'As an elastic category, liberal order can contain almost anything associated with what has traditionally been understood about modern developing societies'. 'The danger in deploying liberal order in this way, as a seemingly trans-historical analytic framework, is that it actually sidesteps the need to confront and elucidate capitalism's changing historical structures'; 'it may well be impossible to discern anything distinctly Canadian about the notion of liberal order'; 'The most serious problem with the liberal order perspective, then, is that it allows mainstream historians to avoid confronting just how critically important it is to name the frontline enemy: capitalism as systematic exploitation and endlessly proliferating oppression.' He adds that McKay's 'elastic understanding of Gramsci's hegemony conflates what Gramsci differentiated as a "separation of powers"'. The elasticity and capitalism argument is at pp. 3–4 and the Gramsci criticism at pp. 4–5. Qualifications kept: 'McKay is not necessarily captive of such tendencies himself' (p. 4), and the book 'stands as an undeniable achievement' (p. 31). This is Palmer's interpretation of the framework. McKay's own position, recorded under lof_mckay_2009 and known here through Fecteau's quotation, distinguishes the two analytically while treating them as historically close: 'Liberal order and capitalism cannot be conflated. Yet, after the 1840s, they also could not be easily separated' (p. 385, as quoted by Fecteau, 2009). That chapter appeared in the same year and is not a reply to Palmer; no direct rejoinder was found. Scope: the essay reviews Reasoning Otherwise and quotes Rebels, Reds, Radicals (2005, p. 84); it does not discuss the 2000 prospectus directly. McKay's reply, if any, was not checked. The critique-audit of 2026-10-14 proposed a group edge cdn_working_class → liberal_order_framework on this text; with the person entry, the person edge carries it and the group edge is not proposed. edge_845 (karl–liberal_order_framework, comparison) stays.

named_group_routes.relationship: Liberalism read as a system of moral regulation and the liberal state as a constitutor of subjectivities (1991–92), beside the liberal order framework's later history of property, the individual and rule
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements, before McKay's prospectus (2000). 'Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State', Labour/Le Travail 30 (1992), pp. 213–222, read in full, endorses Mitchell Dean's argument 'that classical English liberalism was not a negation of state regulation but rather a particular system of economic, social, and moral regulation', so that 'a history of pauperism is also a genealogy of liberalism' (p. 217). She reviews Jean-Marie Fecteau's Un nouvel ordre des choses (1989) as 'a landmark work' whose 'theoretical sophistication' crosses 'the traditional historiographical boundaries separating coercion from benevolence and the state as a whole from charity' (pp. 221–222), but faults its 'moyens de contrôle' as 'a rather functionalist formulation', a 'model of negative class power', and adds that 'These moral codes are not intrinsic to the logic of capital, since capitalism works quite efficiently in different cultural systems' (p. 222). Note 10 (p. 220) cites Fecteau's essay in Greer and Radforth's Colonial Leviathan (1992), and the essay thanks Allan Greer for comments on a draft (p. 222). In the 1991 book (Google Books search-within snippets of the 2008 reissue, 1991 pagination) note 35 (p. 171) cites Bruce Curtis's 'Preconditions of the Canadian State', and she writes that moral regulation 'might be an important social process, which is intertwined with but is not an effect of either the economic or the political' (p. 165) and that 'one has to be sceptical of any claims that envision a clear separation between moral and economic regulation' (p. 166). Reviewers read the book's state argument in the same terms: private philanthropy 'allowed liberal democratic states to adhere to their policy of non-interference in the private sphere' (Loo 1992, p. 278, her paraphrase). Comparison only. The user decided (2026-10-12) that the liberal order framework is 'a different project closer to history of capitalism'; Fecteau and Curtis are shared ground (state formation), not membership. No in-period text by the framework's authors discussing her was read here (McKay's 2000 prospectus is paywalled and unread). edge_848 (liberal_order_framework – moral_regulation) is the field-level comparison. This edge is an editorial comparison of her 1992 argument with the later framework (McKay, 2000); she did not distinguish herself from a framework not yet formulated.

named_group_routes.relationship: Workers' control and class at the centre: Toronto skilled workers' power on the job (1976) and their responses to industrial capitalism (1980), with a periodization by stages of capitalism and a case for class analysis and the materiality of culture (1978–81); contested by Bercuson and Brody (1981) and by feminist critics (1987–2000)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own in-period statements. '“The Honest Workingman” and Workers’ Control', Labour/Le Travailleur 1 (1976), pp. 32–68, read at pp. 32–34 and 58–62: 'Skilled workers in the nineteenth century exercised far more power than we have previously realized. … In Toronto work places, craftsmen employed their monopoly on skill and experience to dictate terms to their employers … which, in modern parlance, gave to these late nineteenth century craftsmen a high degree of workers' control of production' (p. 32); he draws on David Montgomery's 'veterans of industrial life' and on Raymond Williams's 'residual' and 'emergent' (p. 33); 'The custom of workers' control, widely regarded as a right, had become deeply embedded in working class culture' and its defence 'became the major locus of class struggle in the opening decades of the twentieth century' (p. 62). 'The Working Class in Recent Canadian Historical Writing', Acadiensis 7:2 (1978), pp. 116–135, read at pp. 116–117 and 134–135: historians still treat the new study of class 'as little more than interesting additional facts', but 'the new history is well on its way to transforming our understanding of the entire course and structure of Canadian development' (p. 116). 'Labour and Working-Class History in Canada: Prospects in the 1980s', Labour/Le Travailleur 7 (1981), pp. 67–94, read in full: the project 'never excluded the study of unions and labour politics', nor called for history 'simply "written from the bottom up," since it always placed the relationship between classes at the centre of the story' (p. 69); a periodization of 'pre-industrial capitalism to 1850; industrial capitalism, 1850 to the mid-1890s; monopoly capitalism, 1890s to 1929; and crisis and reconstruction, 1930 to the present', offered as 'at best tentative' (p. 74); 'I will certainly stand with scholars such as Thompson and Williams who have argued persuasively for the materiality of culture itself' (p. 85); class 'does have an "objective" side', but '"Class-for-itself," or the failure of the working class to develop such, is almost by definition what working-class history concerns itself with' (pp. 85–86); work on the 1880s found 'a class surprisingly united', in which divisions 'of ethnicity, skill, religion, and even sex were recognized, debated, and for a few years in the 1880s, at least, were overcome', and 'it is now necessary to locate class conflict and class struggle at the centre of modern Canadian history' (p. 89). He places himself among scholars who were 'active in the new left and influenced by the rebirth of Marxist scholarship' (p. 93). Toronto Workers (1980) is unread; Brody quotes its introduction: 'The work will have succeeded to the extent that it provides convincing evidence that the working class was not just "made" but rather was the result of a dialectical interplay of class forces in which it was one of the actors' (p. xviii, as quoted). In-period critics. David Bercuson, in the same issue (pp. 95–96, read), quotes the 1976 Essays definition of the new labour history and notes that 'Kealey's study of Toronto workers contains at least five chapters devoted to working-class and trade-union politics'; his wider objections are recorded under wcreq_bercuson_1981 and edge_919. David Brody, review, Labour/Le Travailleur 8/9 (1981–82), pp. 361–364, read in full: 'Kealey thus lays the foundation, hitherto largely lacking, for a history of the Toronto labour movement' (p. 362), but 'It is in the interpretation of this information that the book founders'; 'Every strike signifies "class conflict," every labour involvement in public life "class politics"' (p. 363); 'Having overreached himself, he has produced only a useable one' (p. 364). Ian McKay, 'Historians, Anthropology, and the Concept of Culture', Labour/Le Travailleur 8/9 (1981–82), cites Kealey's 1981 'defence of the term' (p. 214 n. 88) and argues that working-class culture has 'weak explanatory value' and that Williams's residual and emergent categories 'merely have allowed social historians to indulge in retrospective cheerleading for progressive ideas' (p. 223 and n. 122); Kealey in 1981 called McKay's unpublished paper 'one of the most substantive critiques of Thompson and culturalism' (p. 91 n.). Bettina Bradbury (1987, pp. 35–36, read) and Joan Sangster (2000, p. 133, read): see edge pe138_kealey_rel_05 and the node; Sangster: 'One of the first major collections of the new labour history contained not one article on women' (p. 133, of Kealey and Warrian's Essays, 1976). Desmond Morton (2000, pp. 23–24, read): 'some of the Kealey-Palmer claims for their "new" history were challenged'; 'If, as Kealey insisted, Toronto's working class achieved unity across ethnic and sectarian barriers, it must have been for the briefest of moments in the city contemporaries sometimes called "the Belfast of North America"'. A contribution, not a founding: Freeman (2002) names him in the founding generation of Labour/Le Travail; he presents the work as 'conceived collectively' (1981, p. 68 n. 8). Scope: this edge is Kealey's own contribution; edge_919 carries Palmer's craft culture, edge_886 and edge_890 the Marxist and Thompsonian resources. The Knights of Labor book (1982) is unread and appears in pe138_kealey_rel_05.

named_group_routes.relationship: Schooling, school inspection and the census studied as state formation in the Canadas: education as 'government of the self' (1988), inspection as the making of 'relations of power, authority, domination and exploitation' (1992), the census as 'the making of things to be taken' (2001); work that predates the framework, and that Christie later cites for the point that McKay describes governmentality (2009)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period reviews, read in full; Curtis's books are unread, so his words are the reviewers' quotations with their page references. Davey (Historical Studies in Education 1, 1989, pp. 161–165) on Building the Educational State (1988): 'one of the great strengths of Curtis' approach is his grounding of Foucault's analysis of power and subjectivity within a marxist theory of state formation and cultural forms' (p. 161); he quotes Curtis that 'the construction of the Educational State was accomplished only through the destruction of a prior educational organization and the marginalization of the structure of educational possibilities' (book p. 15), that schooling meant 'the anchoring of the conditions of political governance in the selves of the governed' (no page given), that education 'was not a means to government; education was government: government of the self' (book p. 110) and that 'public education was administered into dominance only through a myriad of local struggles' (book p. 132); Davey notes 'there is no reference to Gramsci or the theory of hegemony in the bibliography or the index' (p. 162) and objects that Curtis 'fails to provide an adequate account of patriarchal relations in the period' (p. 165). Miller (Historical Studies in Education 5, 1993, pp. 123–126) on True Government by Choice Men? (1992) quotes 'Educational inspection was about state formation: the creation, stabilization and normalisation of relations of power, authority, domination and exploitation' (book p. 32) and 'Bureaucratic administration was seen by political liberals as practical education, a ‘normal school’ for the people' (book p. 7); she says Curtis 'carefully distances himself' from a social-control argument (p. 124) and regrets 'the relative invisibility of gender relations' (p. 125). Bryan Palmer (Labour/Le Travail 31, 1993, pp. 365–367): 'In their purpose they can only be applauded; but their search is at times disturbingly narrow' (p. 365); as a 'model' Curtis's account 'is overstated to the point of distorting actual historical relations in the evolution of state and civil society' (p. 366); yet he credits Curtis and Colonial Leviathan with 'the notion that the coming of ‘responsible government’ actually entailed the subversion of the reform strategy of the 1830s' (p. 366). Later readings: Belshaw (2002, read) quotes the census book: 'Census making ... is not in any simple sense the taking of things as they are; in an important sense it is the making of things to be taken' (book p. 305). Christie (Underhill Review 2009, read): 'Here I think we need to be alert to Bruce Curtis's important point that what McKay is really describing is governmentality'; this is Christie's characterisation, and Curtis's own 2009 chapter ('After ‘Canada’') is unread. The edge records a contribution to the strand the atlas calls 'State formation before the framework'; the work predates McKay's prospectus (2000, unread beyond its abstract), and no checked text by McKay names Curtis. The collaboration with Philip Corrigan (1985) is title-level; the moral regulation entry treats this state-formation work as shared ground (edge_848), so no separate Curtis edge to moral_regulation is drawn.

named_group_routes.relationship: Colonial Leviathan (1992, edited with Ian Radforth): mid-nineteenth-century state formation in the Canadas, written before the framework was named, and later faulted by Greer himself for neglecting Indigenous peoples (2019)

In-period reading: Palmer (Labour/Le Travail 31, 1993, read in full) says the volume and Curtis's book 'are searching for the state in pre-Confederation Canada' (p. 365) and finds that 'the collection lacks coherence', while its 'single most important contribution ... also developed by Curtis, is the notion that the coming of ‘responsible government’ actually entailed the subversion of the reform strategy of the 1830s' (p. 366); he names Greer's chapter on the birth of the police (p. 366).
